say.text: A patient with sudden peritonitis reaches the emergency bay. The surgeon wants one test ordered now, at the front door.
Which investigation first?

choices.label: Erect chest X-ray, as the quick first film
CT abdomen, as the most sensitive test
Barium meal, as the familiar contrast study
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test the front door needs in minutes, and which test ranks how few cases it misses.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. The erect chest X-ray is the first investigation in suspected perforation.
It shows free gas under the diaphragm in roughly three-quarters of cases, so it answers the first question quickly.

choices.label: Next
I know the test ladder, skip the teaching

say.text: That choice is not right. CT feels right, because the test that misses least sounds like the one to start with.
But sensitivity ranks tests for doubt; it does not say which test to order first.

choices.label: Try again
Show me why

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the test you start with from the test that settles doubt.

say.text: That choice is not right. Barium is the familiar gut contrast, so it comes to mind before anything else.
A first test for free gas does not involve barium, and in suspected perforation barium must not be given.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the test for free gas, not the contrast you know best.

say.text: Two questions. The first test is the one you order at the front door: quick and available.
The most sensitive test misses the fewest cases, and it is the one to use when the first film leaves doubt.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Same patient, an hour later. The erect film is equivocal and the surgeons still doubt a perforation.
Which test settles the doubt?

choices.label: CT abdomen, since it is the most sensitive
Repeat the erect film, since it was first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test answers a question of doubt, not the question of where to start.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. CT is the most sensitive test and the test of choice when the film leaves doubt.
It also detects small volumes of free gas and fluid, and often localises the site.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. Repeating the first test feels thorough, because it is quick and already requested.
But it carries the same blind spot: a clear film does not exclude perforation, so a repeat cannot settle doubt.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which test answers doubt, not which one starts the work-up.

say.text: An exam stem asks for the investigation of choice in perforated peptic ulcer, with a film and CT both on the list.
Which pairing matches the PYQ key and current practice?

choices.label: PYQ key: erect X-ray. Current practice: CT when in doubt
Both the PYQ key and current practice: erect X-ray
PYQ key: CT. Current practice: erect X-ray
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which frame the stem uses, the exam key or the newer practice, before you pick a test.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. PYQs have expected the erect chest X-ray as the first or initial investigation.
Current practice treats CT abdomen as the most sensitive test, and the test of choice when doubt remains.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. One test for both frames is tempting, because a single name is easier to remember.
The exam key and current practice answer different questions, so each frame needs its own answer.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the stem asks what the exam expects or what current practice does.

say.text: That choice is not right. Swapping the two frames is tempting if you remember CT as the newer, stronger test.
The stem tells you which frame it wants, and the exam key and current practice do not share one answer.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read which source the stem follows before you choose.

say.text: Sudden epigastric pain, board-like rigidity, pulse 112. The erect chest film shows no free gas.
What does that clear film allow you to conclude?

choices.label: The film does not rule out perforation; the work-up goes on
Perforation is very unlikely, so the patient can be observed
Perforation is excluded if the film was taken properly erect
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what fraction of perforations the film can show, and what a rigid belly is still telling you.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. A clear erect film does not exclude perforation.
Free gas is missed in a substantial minority of cases, so a rigid belly keeps the work-up open.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. A clear film reads like a normal result, so it feels safe to close the question.
But a normal film is not a negative test: perforation can be present with no free gas on the film.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether a clear film can ever rule perforation out.

say.text: Free gas shows on the erect film in what share of perforations, and what does that mean for a clear film?

choices.label: About three-quarters, so a quarter show none
Nearly all, so a clear film rules it out
Most, so a clear film makes perforation unlikely
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a test with a miss rate does to a negative result.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Free gas shows in roughly three-quarters of cases; the figure is approximate, and texts vary.
A clear film therefore does not exclude perforation.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. A high share sounds reassuring, so a clear film feels like a closed question.
Free gas is missed in a substantial minority of perforations, so the miss rate is the point.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the film catches every perforation.

say.text: A patient is helped upright and the erect film is taken within seconds. No free gas shows, yet peritonitis is clear.
How long should he sit upright before the film?

choices.label: About 10 minutes, to let the gas rise
Take the film at once, since gas rises
About two minutes, since gas rises quickly
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask how far the gas must travel from the perforation to the diaphragm, and how fast it moves.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Gas must rise through the abdomen, which takes time, so the patient sits for about ten minutes first.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. Gas does rise, so a film taken straight after sitting up feels logical.
But rising takes time, so a film taken too early can miss gas that is still on its way.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask how long the gas needs before it reaches the diaphragm.

say.text: A man with suspected perforation cannot sit up or stand, so an erect film is not possible.
Which abdominal film should be taken instead?

choices.label: Left lateral decubitus film
Supine film, the usual bed view
Right lateral decubitus film
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where gas goes when the patient lies on a given side, and which side lets you see it against the liver.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Lying on the left side lets gas collect between the liver and the lateral abdominal wall, where it can be seen.
That is the view to take when the patient cannot sit up.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. A supine or right-sided film is the usual picture, so the wrong side comes to mind.
But the qualifier is that the patient cannot sit, and the view must let gas rise where the liver can outline it.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so drop the usual picture and work from the patient's position.

say.text: A suspected perforation, and the surgeon wants to know whether it has sealed before deciding on conservative care.
Which contrast study answers that?

choices.label: Water-soluble Gastrografin, to show a seal
Barium sulphate, the familiar GI contrast
Barium, since it shows a leak most clearly
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what each contrast does if it leaks into the peritoneal cavity.

choices.label: Try the question again

say.text: Yes. Water-soluble contrast shows whether the perforation has sealed, which guides conservative care.
Barium is contraindicated when perforation is suspected, because barium peritonitis is severe.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That choice is not right. Barium is the familiar gut contrast, so it feels like the default study.
A leak of barium into the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis, so it is the one medium to avoid here.

choices.label: Try again

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what each medium does if it escapes into the belly.
